clue.text: Ladies' organisation names retiring magician

parts.note: the WI, Women's Institute, is a British women's community organisation

indicators.note: retiring means drawing back, so the word names is read backwards

explanation.surface: A women's group releases the names of members who are stepping down, including a conjuror.
explanation.walkthrough: The Women's Institute is a long-running British women's organisation famous for jam-making; 'retiring' here means going backwards, not leaving office.
explanation.definitionFit: A wise man is a sage or wizard, and the Magi of the Nativity were magicians, the three wise men.

clue.text: High-speed train sound covering mostly quiet first of whistles at the outset

indicators.note: first of picks out only the opening letter of the word whistles
at the outset points to the very start of the word whistles, its opening letter
mostly means the word for a covering loses its final letter

parts.note: a hood is a covering for the head
sh is the call for quiet

explanation.surface: An express train's noise drowns out the guard's whistle as it pulls away.
explanation.definitionFit: The rushing noise of something passing at great velocity, such as an express, is this sound word.

clue.text: PM with tummy upset on board getting slippers

indicators.note: the clue word that signals this step

parts.note: on board means in a steamship, SS, so the other letters go between its two S's

indicators.note: the tummy is the middle of a word, and upset turns those middle letters over

parts.note: Keir Starmer became UK Prime Minister in 2024

explanation.surface: The Prime Minister feels queasy aboard a ship and ends up with house shoes.
explanation.walkthrough: Keir Starmer became UK Prime Minister in 2024; 'tummy upset' flips just the middle two letters of his name, and 'on board' is the crossword convention for going inside a steamship. 'slippers' are not footwear but people who slip.
explanation.definitionFit: Skiers glide or slide over snow, so cryptically they are people who slip along.

clue.text: Person largely mature and fit is compliant

parts.note: man in its old general sense of any human being
aged is mature, cut short by one letter
someone fit for a job is able to do it

explanation.surface: A mostly grown-up, healthy person who does as they are asked.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is the last word, sitting behind 'is', so the first five words are all wordplay — and 'largely' is a trimming instruction, not a comment on how grown-up anybody is.
explanation.definitionFit: Something manageable does what you want without a fight, which is the sense of 'compliant' applied to a thing or a task rather than to a person.

clue.text: Nosy neighbour's opening a half of salmon

indicators.note: opening takes the first letter of each of the words neighbour's and a
half of salmon keeps the first three of its six letters

explanation.surface: A nosy neighbour opens a tin of salmon and shares half.
explanation.definitionFit: Nosy can mean relating to the nose, which is what this adjective describes, as with passages or sprays.

clue.text: Bonaparte mistress's a goddess

indicators.note: Read it as 'has': the two words in front of it have something sitting inside them, running across the join.

parts.note: seven consecutive letters, starting five letters into the emperor's name and finishing inside the second word

explanation.surface: Napoleon's lover, spoken of as though she were divine.
explanation.walkthrough: Napoleon had famous mistresses — Joséphine, Marie Walewska — so the surface sends you hunting for a name. The letters you want are lying still, in order, across the gap between the two words.
explanation.definitionFit: The Greek goddess of the hunt and the moon is one particular Olympian, so 'a goddess' defines by example rather than by class.

clue.text: Share program or no one backs saving time

parts.note: an app is a computer program

indicators.note: saving means keeping something safe inside, here the letter for time
backs means the words no and one are read in reverse order

parts.note: I is the Roman numeral for one

explanation.surface: A scheduling program shares out work, or nobody backs down on saving time.
explanation.definitionFit: To share out is to divide something and allot portions to each party.

clue.text: Change act

definitions.meaning: the verb: weather and milk both do this when they go the other way
the noun: one performer's spot on a music-hall bill

explanation.walkthrough: The two halves are not even the same part of speech — a verb then a noun — which is most of the disguise available in a clue this short.
explanation.definitionFit: Milk turns when it changes, and a turn is a single act in a variety bill — the comic who does five minutes and goes off.

clue.text: Ambitious project — show behind picture?

parts.note: to moon is to bare your backside at somebody
a shot is a photograph, or one frame of film

explanation.surface: A grand scheme that turns out to be baring your backside for the camera.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Behind' is the noun, not the preposition, so 'show behind' is one rude verb rather than an instruction about where a piece goes. The question mark is the setter flagging the joke.
explanation.definitionFit: A moonshot is a wildly ambitious undertaking, the word borrowed from the Apollo programme for any goal that needs a decade and a nation behind it.

clue.text: These fellows wear tight-fitting headgear or small bowlers

parts.note: s is the clothing-label abbreviation for small
in cricket the pacemen are the fast bowlers, the ones who bowl at speed rather than spin

explanation.surface: Fellows in headwear, whether a snug cap or a little bowler hat.
explanation.walkthrough: Bowlers are hats in the surface and cricketers in the wordplay, and 'or' joins the definition to the wordplay instead of offering you a choice between two things.
explanation.definitionFit: Snug helmets and the soft comm caps worn under them are the working headgear of men sent into orbit, so the clue defines them by what is on their heads.

clue.text: 'Old flower', term for bargain hunter

parts.note: o is the standard abbreviation for old
a flower is a thing that flows, meaning a river, and rio is Spanish for one

indicators.note: A term is an end point, the terminus of a line, so it asks for the final letter of the word it points at.

parts.note: the last letter of 'bargain'

explanation.surface: A nickname — 'old flower' — for somebody forever chasing a discount.
explanation.walkthrough: The quotation marks are the setter's tip-off that the flower is not botanical: in crosswords a flower is a thing that flows. Orion is also the capsule that carries this puzzle's Artemis crew.
explanation.definitionFit: The hunter of Greek myth was set among the stars with his belt and his club, so the definition names a constellation by the figure it draws.

clue.text: A sun proven briefly to be unstable

definitions.text: A sun proven briefly to be unstable

indicators.note: unstable letters are not fixed in place, so these letters are rearranged
briefly means cut short, so the last letter is dropped

explanation.surface: A star shown, for a short while, to be on the point of exploding.
explanation.walkthrough: A, SUN and PROVE (proven cut short) are rearranged; read whole, the clue describes the thing itself.
explanation.definitionFit: A supernova is the explosion of a star, typically a sun that has grown unstable at the end of its life.

clue.text: Those last wrestlers maybe united being acknowledged at first

indicators.note: being here means becoming, so one letter turns into another

parts.note: wrestlers struggle with each other, so they are strugglers
U is the abbreviation for united, as in football team names

indicators.note: at first picks out the opening letter of acknowledged

explanation.surface: Wrestlers, perhaps, finally recognised as a united group.
explanation.walkthrough: In STRUGGLERS the U of 'united' is 'being' replaced by the A that starts acknowledged; 'maybe' marks wrestlers as just one example of strugglers.
explanation.definitionFit: Stragglers trail behind the rest, the ones who finish or arrive last.

clue.text: We're told Kite will land in water

indicators.note: What we are told reaches us by ear, so the wordplay describes a noise rather than a spelling.

parts.note: Kite is the setter of this puzzle, so 'Kite will' is him saying 'I will'

explanation.surface: The setter's kite is going to come down in the water.
explanation.walkthrough: Kite is the name at the top of this puzzle, so 'Kite will' is the setter talking about himself. Setters do this often enough that the byline is worth reading before you start.
explanation.definitionFit: An isle is a piece of land with water all round it, which is what the definition says the long way round.

clue.text: She with loads of bananas and pork pies

indicators.note: Going bananas is going wild, and letters told to go wild will not stay in the order they arrived in.

parts.note: the first three letters of the fodder
seven more, the phrase taken whole

explanation.surface: A woman turning up with heaps of fruit and a few pork pies.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bananas' looks like more of the shopping, sitting between the loads and the pies, and it is the one word in the clue giving an order rather than letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Pork pies is Cockney rhyming slang for lies, usually shortened to 'porkies', and it matches the answer in the plural.

clue.text: Pa OK, with a pie and gin cocktail or a bacon sandwich?

indicators.note: A cocktail is several things shaken up together, so the letters offered before it are served in a new order.

parts.note: four letters of fodder
four more
the last three, eleven letters in all

explanation.surface: Dad is content with a pie, a gin cocktail and a bacon sandwich.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cocktail' is the only instruction in a line that otherwise reads as a lunch order, and the eleven letters of fodder are spread over three separate scraps of that menu.
explanation.definitionFit: A poke is an old word for a bag; a bacon sandwich puts the pork inside one, which turns a phrase about buying unseen into a literal description.

clue.text: Trendy Conservative including detailed sale in register

indicators.note: What a thing includes sits inside it, so the letters that follow are pushed in between the two pieces already named.

parts.note: something in is in fashion
a Tory is a British Conservative, the party's nickname since the 17th century
vend is a sale in Chambers, docked of its last letter

explanation.surface: A fashionable Conservative putting an itemised sale into the record.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Detailed' looks like an adjective promising a thorough sale and is really a verb. The two outer pieces already stand in the clue in the order the answer wants them.
explanation.definitionFit: An inventory is the itemised list of what a house or a shop holds, and a register is that same sort of formal list kept as a record.

clue.text: Duke's vessel starting to sink given sailor's not a light body

indicators.note: Something only starting has just its first letter showing, and that letter is the whole of its contribution.

parts.note: d is the standard abbreviation for duke
Noah's ark, the crossword's favourite vessel
the first letter of 'sink'
a tar is an old name for a sailor, from the tarpaulin clothing they wore

explanation.surface: A duke's boat begins to go down, and the sailor proves to be no lightweight.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not a light body' looks like a remark about the sailor's build and is the definition, which leaves everything in front of it as four pieces laid end to end.
explanation.definitionFit: A dark star is a stellar body that gives out no visible light, so the definition describes it plainly and leaves the astronomy for you to supply.

clue.text: Standard finish for screen

parts.note: par is the standard score for a golf hole, and 'up to par' means up to standard
to close a meeting is to finish it

explanation.surface: The ordinary paint finish applied to a screen.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is a church word: parcloses are the screens that shut a side chapel off from the nave. Both wordplay words are everyday ones, which is what hides the join between them.
explanation.definitionFit: A parclose is the carved screen that fences off a chapel or a tomb inside a church, so the definition is the word's plain architectural sense.

clue.text: Anyway, slave with talent for cooking

indicators.note: Cooking mixes its ingredients past recognition, so the letters in front of it come out in a different arrangement.

parts.note: five letters of fodder
six more, eleven in all

explanation.surface: A kitchen slave who happens to have a real gift for cooking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'For cooking' reads as the thing the slave is good at, and 'cooking' is the instruction. Eleven letters is a lot to hold in the head, so count them against the enumeration first.
explanation.definitionFit: 'At all events' means whatever happens, in any case — the job 'anyway' does when you wave an objection aside and carry on regardless.

clue.text: Craftsman makes good partner

parts.note: g is the standard abbreviation for good
the partner you are romantically attached to

explanation.surface: A skilled craftsman turning out to be somebody's ideal partner.
explanation.walkthrough: Victor Glover pilots Artemis II, and three of his crewmates are at 1, 20 and 21. 'Makes' is only joinery, though the trade in the definition does literally make things.
explanation.definitionFit: A glover makes and sells gloves — Shakespeare's father was one — so the definition names a trade rather than any particular skill.

clue.text: German/English name for leprosy pioneer

parts.note: Hans is the stock German first name, their equivalent of John
e is the standard abbreviation for English
n is the standard abbreviation for name

explanation.surface: A name that serves in German and in English, worn by a pioneer of leprosy research.
explanation.walkthrough: The slash does no work beyond the surface: German and English are two separate pieces of wordplay rather than one hyphenated nationality. Jeremy Hansen is Artemis II's Canadian mission specialist.
explanation.definitionFit: The Norwegian doctor who identified the leprosy bacterium in 1873 gave the disease the name it carries in medicine today, and 'pioneer' points at him.

clue.text: German scientist has floor with central heating

parts.note: to floor somebody is to knock them out, and KO is boxing shorthand for it
ch is the estate agent's abbreviation for central heating

explanation.surface: A German scientist whose flat has floors and central heating.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Floor' is a verb, not a storey — to floor a man is to knock him down. Christina Koch flies on Artemis II, joining three more of that crew in this grid.
explanation.definitionFit: The bacteriologist who identified the bacilli behind tuberculosis and cholera was German, so the definition points at one particular scientist rather than the class.

clue.text: Not ideal, he reused tissues

indicators.note: Something reused is put back to work in a new arrangement, which is what happens to the letters offered in front of it.

parts.note: ten letters of fodder, the whole opening phrase

explanation.surface: Somebody less than ideal, using the same paper tissues twice over.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tissues' reads as the paper kind and means the biological kind, which is the whole distance between the surface and the answer. Ten letters, so count them before moving any.
explanation.definitionFit: Endothelia are the thin cell layers lining blood vessels and the heart, so the definition names them by their biological class, in the plural.

clue.text: Piece of gold circle

parts.note: or is gold in heraldry, straight from the French
a bit is a piece of something

explanation.surface: A fragment broken off a gold ring.
explanation.walkthrough: The two wordplay words arrive in the opposite order to the letters they give, so 'piece of gold' has to be read as the piece going after the gold rather than before it.
explanation.definitionFit: An orbit is the closed loop one body travels round another, so the definition is the shape it traces rather than any drawn ring.

clue.text: Bird or rabbit

definitions.meaning: the ornithological reading: a family of small perching birds named for their scolding call
the slang reading: to rabbit on is to talk at length

explanation.surface: A bird and a rabbit, named in the same breath.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Rabbit' is a verb here. It comes from the rhyming slang rabbit and pork, meaning talk, and nothing in the clue admits the two words are animals in the surface only.
explanation.definitionFit: A chat is a small songbird — stonechat, whinchat — and to rabbit is British slang for talking on and on, which is a chat by another name.

clue.text: It's fine, so they say now, very thin, evenly-divided dress

definitions.text: It's fine, so they say now

parts.note: too means very, as in not too bad

indicators.note: divide the word evenly in two and keep only the first half

parts.note: to dress hair is to comb it

explanation.surface: Someone calls a very thin, neatly split garment fine nowadays.
explanation.walkthrough: The proper phrase is fine-tooth comb, but people say fine toothcomb, hence 'so they say'. Thin halved gives TH.
explanation.definitionFit: A toothcomb is a comb with fine closely-set teeth, which people commonly call a fine toothcomb.

clue.text: Idiots' heads not used at the beginning

indicators.note: The letter standing at the front is the one left out, so the word starts a letter later than it should.

parts.note: a loaf is a head in British slang — 'use your loaf' means use your head — so heads in the plural are loaves

explanation.surface: Fools who fail to use their heads before they begin.
explanation.walkthrough: Nothing in the line looks like an instruction until you notice that the last five words are one, and the surface goes on reading as a complaint about people who never think first.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer is an old plural of 'oaf', the big clumsy stupid one, so the definition matches it in both sense and number.

clue.text: Note record for return of 8

parts.note: re is the second note of the sol-fa scale, do re mi
an entry in a ledger is the record of a single transaction

explanation.surface: Making a note of the record set by something coming back.
explanation.walkthrough: The 8 is a cross-reference to 8 down, so the definition only opens up once that one is solved — a habit worth expecting whenever a grid has a theme running through it.
explanation.definitionFit: Coming back down through the atmosphere is what a spacecraft does at the end of a flight, and 8 down is the crew making that return.

clue.text: Check score of 1 in game

parts.note: a Test is the five-day international match at the top of cricket
one run is the smallest score a cricket batter can add

explanation.surface: Looking up the one-point score from a game.
explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are cricket: a single run, scored in a Test match. The clue names them in the reverse of the order the answer needs them.
explanation.definitionFit: A test run is a trial to see whether something works, and 'check' is that same noun: the check you give a system before you trust it.
